title: Training for competition
summary: How to bring competition into training: full rounds, your own routine, the time limits of your discipline and mild pressure that grows step by step.

body.html: A competition feels different: new targets, shooters you do not know, a referee and nerves. To make this feel familiar, many coaches suggest running some sessions as if they were a competition.
Shoot full rounds and keep score. Do not ask for a target again after you miss it, and shoot the targets in the order of the menu.
That is how a competition runs: a missed target is not thrown again, and the targets come in the order the menu lists them. The menu is the board that shows which targets you shoot and in what order.

html.sporting: A round on one layout is 25 targets: 15 singles and 5 doubles (Chapter 2 · Number of traps and targets per layout type).
html.compak: A round is 25 targets, 5 at each of the 5 stations (Chapter 17 · A round: 25 targets, 5 per station).

body.html: Use your pre-shot routine on each target: the same steps in the same order. Studies of routines, mostly in other sports, suggest that athletes who use one do better, also when they are nervous. This probably applies to clay shooting too. More in Pre-shot routine: the same steps in the same order.

Doing the steps in the same order each time seems to matter more than taking exactly the same number of seconds. That suits clay shooting, because the time between your call and the target can differ from target to target. In Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™ a person releases the target, and so it is in Compak® Sporting with a manual release. The rules set only an upper limit for this delay. Only a sonopull in Compak® Sporting, a device that releases the target when it hears your call, keeps the delay fixed. The exact times are below.

html.sporting: Before the call the gun is not mounted. The heel of the stock, the top corner of the end that goes into your shoulder, touches your body. The top of the stock stays below the jacket line. It is a line marked across your vest or jacket 25 cm below the shoulder axis; the shoulder axis is an imaginary horizontal line through both shoulders. Keep this ready position (gun down, ready to mount) until the target is released and you can see it (Chapter 3 · Ready position: feet and gun, Chapter 3 · The 25 cm marking line on the jacket).
html.compak: The gun position at the call is free: mounted or not. Each target is shot with the gun at the shoulder. There is no jacket line (Chapter 17 · Gun position when calling).

body.html: Practise the way each shot begins in your discipline: the gun position, the call and the wait for the target.

html.sporting: You have at most 15 seconds between singles or between doubles (Chapter 7 · 15 seconds between targets). After your call the referee gives a signal to the trapper, the person who releases the targets. The target comes within 3 seconds of the referee's signal (Chapter 5 · Calling for the target and the 3-second release).
html.compak: You have at most 10 seconds to call, counted from the shot at the previous station's target (Chapter 21 · 10 seconds to call: warning, then penalty). The target leaves within 3 seconds of the call with a manual release, or half a second after it with a sonopull (voice release) (Chapter 2 · Releasing targets: manual, remote, sonopull).

body.html: Time your routine in training: it should fit the time limit without rushing. If the targets are released by hand, ask the trapper to vary the delay a little, so you learn to stay ready while you wait. More about the rules: The call, time limits and lateness.

Add mild pressure, step by step: a score that counts, someone watching, a small stake. Research on pressure training suggests that people who practise under mild pressure keep their skill better when the pressure is real. The studies come from other sports and tasks, so this probably applies to clay shooting too.

html: Five in a row: choose one target and stay with it until you break five in a row; a miss starts the count again.
A test round: a full round with a score, in the menu order, with no repeated targets and with the time limit of your discipline.
An audience: ask a friend to watch, act as the referee and announce the results aloud.
A small stake: a friendly match in which, for example, the loser buys the coffee.
A shoot-off drill. A shoot-off is the extra shooting that decides a tie. After a round, at short notice, shoot one more full round and, if you like, a sudden-death series that ends at the first miss.

body.html: A real shoot-off is held only for the first three places. In both disciplines it is 25 targets and, if the shooters are still level, sudden death: the first to miss is out (Chapter 18 · Shoot-off for the top three; ties below, Chapter 18 · Shoot-off format and sudden death, Chapter 14 · Shoot-offs for the top three: 25 targets, then sudden death).

How to fit this into normal training. Many coaches keep technique work for the first part of a session and add one pressure task near the end, once or twice a week. While you are learning a new movement, leave the pressure out until it feels settled. If technique falls apart, make the task easier rather than pushing on.
A competition is a poor place for experiments. Test a new choke, cartridge or lens in training first.

Agree on the plan in advance. Coaching, giving a competitor advice during a competition, is not allowed in either discipline. If the referee decides that coaching is happening, the shooter gets a yellow card, and the person coaching is sent out of the shooting area (Chapter 8 · No coaching during competition, Chapter 21 · No coaching during competition).

html.sporting: Before the event nobody may practise on the competition layouts, so practise on other ones (Chapter 15 · No practice on competition layouts).
html.compak: Before the event you may practise on the competition trajectories, but with a different trajectory setting table: a ready-made menu that says which traps throw the targets at each station. So during practice you see the same targets, but in other combinations than on the day (Chapter 6 · Practice on competition trajectories). At continental and world championships official practice opens on the Saturday before the championship (Chapter 6 · Championships: official practice from the Saturday before).

notes.html: Raise the pressure only as fast as the shooter's technique holds. If the mount or the tempo changes, step back to an easier task. Before the event, agree on the plan; during it you may not coach.
During a competition, pass on only what the referee and the officials say. Translating a coach's tips to a shooter can count as coaching.

key_points.html: Run some sessions as a competition: full rounds, a score and no repeated targets
The same routine on each target, timed against the limit of your discipline
Sporting™: gun down, stock below the jacket line until the target appears; Compak® Sporting: gun position free
Add mild pressure step by step, once or twice a week
No coaching during a competition: agree on the plan before the start

did_you_know.html: Many shooters use small local competitions as training: they practise their routine and find out which targets break down under pressure.

quiz.q: In Sporting™, how much time do you have between singles?
quiz.explain: Going over the limit earns a warning first, then penalties. In Compak® Sporting you have at most 10 seconds to call.

quiz.q: In which discipline must the stock stay below the jacket line until the target appears?
quiz.explain: In Compak® Sporting the gun position at the call is free, and there is no jacket line.

quiz.q: How do studies suggest adding pressure to training?

options.text: As much as possible from the first session
Only in the week before the competition
Mild at first, then growing step by step

quiz.explain: Mild pressure that grows slowly lets technique hold while you get used to it.
